text: Imagine a forger learning to paint banknotes and a bank inspector learning to catch fakes. Each improves by studying the other's mistakes, and if they keep at it, the forgeries become hard to tell from the real thing. That contest is the whole idea of a generative adversarial network.

Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduced GANs in twenty fourteen. The generator takes random noise and turns it into a sample, such as an image. The discriminator takes either a real example or a generated one, and outputs the probability that it is real. The generator never sees a written-down target for what a good image looks like; its only signal is the discriminator's judgement, passed back to it as gradients.

Training is a game played over a single value. The discriminator tries to maximise the log-probability it gives to the right answer on real and on generated examples, and the generator tries to minimise that same value. The paper showed that for a fixed generator, the best discriminator outputs the data density divided by the sum of the data and generator densities, and that against this best discriminator, the generator is minimising the Jensen-Shannon divergence between its distribution and the data's. The game is won when the two distributions match.

In practice there is a snag. Early in training the discriminator rejects fakes easily, and the generator's original loss then gives it almost no gradient. The same paper suggested the fix that became standard: train the generator to maximise the log-probability that the discriminator calls its samples real, which pushes hardest exactly when the generator is losing.

GANs became famous both for sharp images and for being temperamental. The two players can circle each other instead of settling, and the generator can fall into mode collapse, producing a few convincing outputs over and over instead of the full variety of the data, like a forger who only ever paints one banknote. A long line of later work, from careful architectures to new losses, set out to tame this.

Compared with the models of the last two lessons, a GAN generates in a single pass, which makes it fast, but it has no likelihood and no reconstruction loss to keep it honest. Diffusion models are slower, yet they train with a stable regression objective and cover the variety of the data better, which is part of why they overtook GANs for many image tasks. The adversarial idea survives, though, for example as an extra loss that sharpens the decoders of the image autoencoders used in latent diffusion.
That completes our tour of generative models. The next module turns to learning from rewards rather than from examples, beginning with agents, rewards and Markov decision processes.
